in_text_mentions: diagnosis. Although its pathogenesis remains controversial, there are indications that it is triggered by local trauma and microangiopathic changes.42-45 Diabetic dermopathy appears as pigmented pretibial spots46,47 predominantly bilaterally, as erythematous and rounded plaques or papules. In a few days, they evolve to a brownish tone, covered by fine scales44 (Figure 4). However, it can occur in less typical body areas, such as the forearms, thighs, and lateral malleoli, making the differential diagnosis of dermatophytosis important.48 In a few patients, this can be complicated by ulceration.

findings.label: Atrophic skin surface
findings.evidence: in-text: 'with atrophic scars'; atrophic, slightly depressed patches visible in the image

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the pretibial region showing multiple light-brown, irregular, atrophic macules/patches typical of diabetic dermopathy (shin spots), bilaterally distributed, in a 34-year-old man with long-standing diabetes; the caption and in-text explicitly attribute these lesions to diabetic dermopathy. The same panel also shows central crusting over a ruptured bulla (bullosis diabeticorum), a co-existing non-target condition; this is not a separate comparison panel of another disease, so the panel still qualifies for the target disease, but the presence of the second disorder lowers confidence. No ethnicity stated; age from in-text mention.
panels.attribution_text: Brzezinski et al. Diabetic dermopathy ("shin spots") and diabetic bullae ("bullosis diabeticorum") at the same patient.. Pakistan journal of medical sciences 2015. doi:10.12669/pjms.315.7521. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Diabetic dermopathy and crusts over large bullae on bilateral pretibial areas.
in_text_mentions: A 34-year-old man, with long history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and moderate obesity presented to Dermatology Unit for diagnosis of his skin lesions. On clinical examination multiple, light brown, irregular patches, with atrophic scars and crusts over large bullae were observed on the anterior aspect of both legs (Fig.1). The skin lesions were totally asymptomatic, no previous trauma reported by the patient, no drug intake apart from insulin. Thepatient reported the appearance of lesions in crops, over the last one year, despite good control of metabolic status.
